title: Pauri 31: storehouses everywhere
hook: aasan loe loe: His seat and storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all (Japji 31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: viddaan, wonder, and your line, seen, though unseen. Today, the last of the four stanzas for the yogis.

You've seen the photos: grocery shelves stripped bare because everyone got scared at the same time. Toilet paper gone, bread gone, one sad can of beans. Fear of running out makes people grab. Now cut open one apple and count the seeds. Five, maybe eight. Each could grow a tree, and each tree could drop hundreds of apples a year for decades. One apple holds an orchard. The world is stocked in a way that's hard to take in, and most days it goes unnoticed behind the worry about the shelves. Pauri 31 is about the storehouses.
screen: `EMPTY SHELVES.` → `ONE APPLE, EIGHT SEEDS.` → `AN ORCHARD INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Pauri 31 is short, and it opens with a yogi's word. Aasan loe loe bhanddaar. Aasan is a seat, the mat or skin a yogi carried and sat on to meditate. Wherever he went, his aasan went too, and that spot became his place. Guru Nanak says the One's aasan is loe loe, in world after world. There's no single spot to travel to. Bhanddaar: storehouses. In Pauri 29, compassion was the bhanddaaran, the keeper of the stores. In Pauri 30, one of the three powers was the bhanddaaree, the one who sustains. Now the storehouses themselves are in every world. Then today's line: jo kichh paaiaa su ekaa vaar. Whatever was put in, was put in once. Commentators read it as a creation already provided for: the stores filled at the start, not in a panic every morning. Kar kar vekhai sirjanhaar: having made it, the Creator watches over it, the same care as yesterday. Sache kee saachee kaar: true is the work of the True One. And the refrain, one last time: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. With that, Nanak's answer to the yogis is complete. Their earrings, their meal, their horn, their seat: each one turned toward the One who is everywhere. Tomorrow, the Japji starts to climb.
screen: `AASAN — THE YOGI'S SEAT, EVERYWHERE.` · `BHANDDAAR — STOREHOUSES IN EVERY WORLD.` · `FILLED ONCE, NOT IN A PANIC.` · `THE MAKER WATCHES WHAT WAS MADE.` · then, large: `FILLED ONCE, FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Look at one place you can see or picture, a window with a tree in it, a kitchen shelf, your own hands, as a storehouse: leaves, light, grain, breath, years of work in your fingers. Don't count what's missing; notice what's already there, and let it be more than you expected. Then breathe, one easy breath after another, drawing from a store you didn't fill.
Aasan, the yogi's seat. His seat and His storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all, and the Maker watches over what was made. The last answer to the yogis.
Your line: filled once, for all. The stores were full from the start. Day two hundred fifteen, done.

screen: `DAY 215 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 32, SOUND: IK DOO JEEBHAU.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 31 closes the four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and its picture of storehouses in every world is often recalled as a teaching on trust and contentment.

fork.setup: a yogi carries his seat, his aasan, from place to place. where does Pauri 31 say the One's seat is?
fork.reveal: aasan loe loe: in every world. there's no single spot to travel to; the seat is everywhere.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 31: His seat and storehouses are in every world.

trapdoor: what you thought: God has warehouses.
what it means: what creation needs was placed in it, in every world, once and for all, and the Maker watches over it.
what a scholar hears: aasan is the Nath yogi's seat; bhanddaar completes a storeroom thread that runs from the bhanddaaran of Pauri 29 through the bhanddaaree of Pauri 30.
